content.summary: Read a short business phone conversation about changing an appointment and passing on a message. Practise finding the reason for a call, noting important details, and understanding polite requests and promises to follow up.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Use polite requests such as “Could I speak to...?” and “Would you mind...?” Learn how to pass on a message with “Could you tell her that...” and how to explain a call with “I'm calling to...” or “I'm calling about...”.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Learn expressions for connecting a caller, asking someone to wait, leaving a message, changing an appointment and contacting someone again.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim the conversation first to find its main purpose. Then scan for names, dates, times and actions. Check who says each line before deciding who will do something.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short business phone conversation.
Locate details such as a caller's name, a meeting time and a requested action.
Recognize polite requests and phrases used to explain the purpose of a call.
Understand how one person can pass a message to someone who is unavailable.

contextWarmup.prompt: You call an office, but the person you need is away from their desk. What is a useful next step?
options: Ask if you can leave a message.
End the call without saying anything.
Ask the receptionist to guess when the person will return.
contextWarmup.explanation: Asking to leave a message is polite and gives the person a way to receive your information later.

rules: Use “Could I speak to...” to ask politely for a person or department.
Use “I'm calling to...” before an action, such as confirming an appointment. Use “I'm calling about...” before a topic.
When passing on a message, use “Could you tell him or her that...” or “Could you ask him or her to...”
Use “hold the line” when asking a caller to wait, and explain what you will do.
When confirming a new appointment, repeat the day and time so both people have the same details.

commonTrap.explanation: A message can include several details, so do not confuse the person who called with the person who needs to receive the message. Check the names and actions carefully.
commonTrap.wrong: The caller asks to speak to Ms. Chen, so Ms. Chen is the person who called.
commonTrap.correct: The caller is the person making the call. Ms. Chen is the person the caller wants to speak to.

content.passageTitle: A Call to Confirm a Meeting
paragraphs: At 10:15 on Tuesday morning, Daniel called Northway Design to speak to Ms. Chen in the marketing department. Receptionist Priya answered and asked, “Could I ask who's calling, please?” Daniel introduced himself and said he was calling to follow up on an email about a product meeting. Priya asked him to hold the line while she checked whether Ms. Chen was available.

Ms. Chen was in another meeting, so Daniel chose to leave a message. He asked Priya to tell her that he could not attend their Thursday appointment at 2 p.m. because he had to visit a client. He also asked whether it would be possible to reschedule the meeting to Friday morning. Priya wrote down Daniel's name, company and phone number.

Priya said she would make sure Ms. Chen got the message as soon as she returned to her desk. Daniel thanked her and asked if he could expect a reply before the end of the day. Priya said she could not promise a time, but she would ask Ms. Chen to get back to him. At 3:30, Daniel called again. Ms. Chen answered and confirmed a new meeting time: Friday at 10 a.m.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Professional Telephone Messages and Follow-Up Notes

content.summary: This guide teaches you how to write clear telephone message slips and short follow-up emails. You will learn polite sentence formulas for stating reasons for calling, reporting messages accurately, and confirming appointments.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Stating the Purpose of a Call
blueprintItems.formula: I am calling to + base verb OR I am calling about + noun phrase
blueprintItems.example: I am calling to confirm our meeting on Thursday afternoon.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Relaying Messages with Indirect Requests
blueprintItems.formula: Could you ask + object pronoun / name + to + base verb...?
blueprintItems.example: Could you ask Mr. Davis to call me back before five o'clock?

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Structuring a Follow-Up Email Note
blueprintItems.formula: Polite Opening + As discussed, [details] + Next Step / Call to Action + Sign-off
blueprintItems.example: Dear Ms. Chen, thank you for your call today. As discussed, our appointment is scheduled for Friday at 10:00 a.m. Please let me know if you need any further information.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a comma after introductory dependent clauses or transitional phrases when writing follow-up notes.
mechanicsRules.badExample: As discussed on the phone I have attached the updated report.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: As discussed on the phone, I have attached the updated report.
mechanicsRules.why: Introductory phrases need a comma to separate them from the main subject and verb.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use a gerund (verb ending in -ing) directly after 'Would you mind'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Would you mind to send me the file again?
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Would you mind sending me the file again?
mechanicsRules.why: The verb 'mind' takes a gerund complement, not a to-infinitive.

mechanicsRules.rule: In indirect reporting clauses, keep normal statement word order (Subject + Verb) instead of question word order.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Could you tell me when does the call start?
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Could you tell me when the call starts?
mechanicsRules.why: An embedded clause within a polite request is not an independent question, so it does not use auxiliary inversion.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine these two sentences into one using 'as soon as':

practicumQuestions.hint: Place 'as soon as' before the present tense clause: '...as soon as he returns...'

I will give Mr. Baker your message as soon as he returns to the office.
As soon as Mr. Baker returns to the office, I will give him your message.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Clear and Confident Phone Calls

content.summary: Practise speaking clearly and politely on business calls. Use a calm pace, listen carefully, record names and key details, and repeat important information to check that you heard it correctly.
content.audioGuidance: Speak at a steady pace and pronounce each word clearly. Let your voice rise gently when asking a yes-or-no question, such as “Could you hold the line?” Use falling intonation for statements and confirmations. Pause briefly between a caller's name, phone number, and message.

pillars.name: Clear Word Stress
pillars.target: Stress the important syllable in common telephone words
pillars.explanation: Say re-SCHED-ule and CON-firm with a clear main stress. Correct stress helps listeners understand you, especially on a phone call.

pillars.name: Polite Intonation
pillars.target: Use a rising tone for polite questions
pillars.explanation: Let your voice rise at the end of questions such as “Would you like to leave a message?” Keep your voice warm and professional.

pillars.name: Careful Message Taking
pillars.target: Speak clearly when repeating names, times, and numbers
pillars.explanation: Pause between details, then check them with the caller. For example, say, “That’s Tuesday at two thirty, correct?”

pillars.name: Natural Call Rhythm
pillars.target: Use short phrases and helpful pauses
pillars.explanation: Do not rush through a message. Pause after phrases such as “I’ll check” and “I’ll get back to you” so the caller can follow your meaning.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: In “confirm,” the stress is on the second syllable. In “confirmation,” it moves to the third syllable.
The main stress stays on “sched” in both words.
Keep the first syllable of “message” strong, and give “taking” its own stress.
The main stress stays on “va” when you add “un” to make “unavailable.”

drills.targetText: Could you hold the line while I check if she is available?

drills.targetText: I’ll put you through to the sales department.
drills.phonetic: /aɪl pʊt juː θruː tə ðə seɪlz dɪˈpɑːtmənt/

drills.targetText: I’ll get back to you by this afternoon.

drills.hint: Pause briefly after “calling” and stress “follow up” and “meeting time.”

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 20 seconds about a time you made or received an important phone call.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell me about an important phone call you remember.
storyPoints: Who you called or who called you, and why
What information you needed to give or receive
How the call ended and what happened next
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I called the office to confirm my appointment, and the receptionist told me the new time.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Tell the events in a clear order. Use past simple forms and include the reason for the call.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 20 seconds about a time a plan or appointment changed.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Describe a time you had to change an appointment or meeting.
storyPoints: What the original appointment was and when it was planned
Why you needed to change the time
How you contacted the other person and confirmed the new time
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I called to reschedule the meeting, and we agreed to speak again next Wednesday.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ kɔːld tə ˌriːˈʃedjuːl ðə ˈmiːtɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use past simple to describe what happened and clear time phrases to explain the change.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live call. Ask the receptionist to connect you to the accounts department.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are calling a company about an invoice. The receptionist answers and needs to know which department you want.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the caller. Greet the receptionist, say why you are calling, and politely ask to be put through to the accounts department.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Could you put me through to the accounts department, please?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /kʊd juː pʊt miː θruː tə ði əˈkaʊnts dɪˌpɑːtmənt pliːz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a polite request and explain the reason for your call in one clear sentence.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live call. Ask the caller to hold while you check whether a colleague is available.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You work at a reception desk. A caller asks to speak to Ms Patel, and you need a moment to check her availability.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the receptionist. Greet the caller, ask them to hold the line, and say you will check if Ms Patel is available.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Could you hold the line for a moment while I check if she is available?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /kʊd juː həʊld ðə laɪn fər ə ˈməʊmənt waɪl aɪ tʃek ɪf ʃiː ɪz əˈveɪləbl/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a polite question and speak calmly so the caller knows what you are doing.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live call. Leave a short message for someone who is not available.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You call a supplier to ask about a delivery. The person you need is away from their desk, and the receptionist offers to take a message.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the caller. Give your name, explain what you are following up on, and ask the person to call you back.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Please tell Mr Lee I’m calling to follow up on our delivery.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /pliːz tel ˈmɪstə liː aɪm ˈkɔːlɪŋ tə ˈfɒləʊ ʌp ɒn aʊə dɪˈlɪvəri/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Include the purpose of your call and make your request easy to understand.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live follow-up call. Suggest a new time and check that the other person agrees.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are calling a colleague because you cannot attend a meeting at the planned time. You need to arrange a different time.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the caller. Apologise briefly, suggest rescheduling to next Wednesday at ten, and ask the colleague to confirm.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Could we reschedule the meeting to next Wednesday at ten?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /kʊd wiː ˌriːˈʃedjuːl ðə ˈmiːtɪŋ tə nekst ˈwenzdeɪ æt ten/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Give the proposed day and time clearly, then ask a question to confirm the new arrangement.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Use each phrase in a complete sentence: “put someone through,” “hold the line,” “get back to someone,” “reschedule,” “follow up on,” and “leave a message.”

practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I’m calling to follow up on the order, and I’ll get back to you this afternoon.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪm ˈkɔːlɪŋ tə ˈfɒləʊ ʌp ɒn ði ˈɔːdə/

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practise polite requests and future promises. Change direct instructions into polite questions, then say what you will do next.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ask someone to wait, ask to change a meeting time, and promise to call back.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Could you hold the line? I’ll check the schedule and get back to you.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /kʊd juː həʊld ðə laɪn aɪl tʃek ðə ˈʃedjuːl ænd ɡet bæk tə juː/

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each word clearly and stress the correct syllable: “confirm,” “reschedule,” “message,” and “available.”
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Repeat the words, then use them in a short telephone message.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Please confirm the rescheduled meeting with the available manager.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /pliːz kənˈfɜːm ðə ˌriːˈʃedjuːld ˈmiːtɪŋ wɪð ði əˈveɪləbl ˈmænɪdʒə/

reading.question: Why did Daniel call Northway Design?
options: To follow up on an email about a product meeting
To apply for a job in the marketing department
To ask Priya for directions to the office
reading.answer: To follow up on an email about a product meeting
reading.explanation: Daniel said he was calling to follow up on an email about a product meeting.

reading.question: Who answered Daniel's first call?
options: Ms. Chen
Priya
A client
reading.explanation: The passage says that receptionist Priya answered the call.

reading.question: What did Priya ask Daniel to do while she checked if Ms. Chen was available?
options: Hold the line
Call a client
Send another email
reading.explanation: Priya asked Daniel to hold the line while she checked.

reading.question: Why could Daniel not attend the Thursday appointment?
options: He had to visit a client.
He was going on holiday.
He had another meeting with Priya.
reading.answer: He had to visit a client.
reading.explanation: Daniel asked Priya to pass on that he had to visit a client.

reading.question: What time was the original appointment?
options: Thursday at 2 p.m.
Friday at 10 a.m.
Tuesday at 10:15 a.m.
reading.explanation: Daniel said he could not attend the Thursday appointment at 2 p.m.

reading.question: What details did Priya write down?
options: Daniel's name, company and phone number
Ms. Chen's address and email password
The client's name and home address
reading.answer: Daniel's name, company and phone number
reading.explanation: The passage says Priya wrote down Daniel's name, company and phone number.

reading.question: What did Daniel ask Priya to do?
options: Ask Ms. Chen if they could meet on Friday morning
Cancel the meeting without telling Ms. Chen
Send the client to Northway Design
reading.answer: Ask Ms. Chen if they could meet on Friday morning
reading.explanation: Daniel asked whether it would be possible to reschedule the meeting to Friday morning.

reading.question: What did Priya say she would do?
options: Make sure Ms. Chen got the message
Confirm a new time without asking Ms. Chen
Call Daniel before lunch
reading.answer: Make sure Ms. Chen got the message
reading.explanation: Priya said she would make sure Ms. Chen got the message when she returned to her desk.

reading.question: When did Daniel call again?
reading.explanation: The final paragraph says Daniel called again at 3:30.

reading.question: What new meeting time did Ms. Chen confirm?
options: Friday at 10 a.m.
Thursday at 2 p.m.
Tuesday at 10:15 a.m.
reading.explanation: Ms. Chen confirmed that the new meeting would be on Friday at 10 a.m.

reading.question: According to the workplace policy, what is the primary consequence of missing a project milestone?
options: The project lead must submit a revised timeline and conduct a risk assessment.
The entire development team is immediately replaced by external contractors.
All project funding is automatically cancelled without further review.
Clients are notified only after the product is officially deployed.
reading.answer: The project lead must submit a revised timeline and conduct a risk assessment.
reading.explanation: Standard corporate policy dictates remediation through timeline review and risk mitigation.

reading.question: Which connector indicates a contrast between two independent clauses?
options: Nevertheless
Furthermore
Consequently
Similarly
reading.explanation: 'Nevertheless' signals contrast or concession, equivalent to 'however'.

reading.question: What does the author imply by stating 'the transition required considerable organizational agility'?
options: The company had to adapt rapidly to unexpected structural changes.
Employees refused to learn modern technological software.
The executive leadership considered the project an outright failure.
No further organizational adjustments would be necessary in the future.
reading.answer: The company had to adapt rapidly to unexpected structural changes.
reading.explanation: 'Agility' signifies the capacity to pivot and respond flexibly to change.

reading.question: Identify the sentence that correctly utilizes the Third Conditional:
options: If we had anticipated the market demand, we would have expanded production sooner.
If we anticipate the market demand, we will expand production.
If we had anticipated the market demand, we will have expanded production.
If we anticipated the market demand, we would expand production sooner.
reading.answer: If we had anticipated the market demand, we would have expanded production sooner.
reading.explanation: Third conditional formula: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

reading.question: Why did the client request an amendment to the contractual agreement?
options: To ensure delivery milestones aligned with their internal quarterly budget cycles.
Because they intended to terminate all business relations immediately.
To eliminate all warranty protections and technical support clauses.
Because the initial contract was drafted without legal counsel.
reading.answer: To ensure delivery milestones aligned with their internal quarterly budget cycles.
reading.explanation: Contract amendments in B2 business scenarios typically align scope with financial planning.

writing.instruction: Turn this direct request into a polite indirect message request starting with 'Could you ask John to...':
writing.promptText: Tell John: 'Please call me back before lunch.'
writing.hint: Use 'Could you ask John to' followed by the base verb phrase.
targetAnswers: Could you ask John to call me back before lunch?
Could you ask John to please call me back before lunch?
writing.explanation: To make an indirect request, use 'Could you ask + name + to + base verb'.

writing.instruction: Correct the punctuation and capitalization in this opening line of a follow-up message:
writing.promptText: dear ms taylor thank you for your phone call yesterday
writing.hint: Add a comma after the salutation and end with a full stop. Capitalize proper nouns.
targetAnswers: Dear Ms. Taylor, thank you for your phone call yesterday.
Dear Ms Taylor, thank you for your phone call yesterday.
writing.explanation: Formal salutations require capitalization of titles and surnames, followed by a comma.

writing.instruction: Combine the two sentences into one using the conjunction 'so that':
writing.promptText: I am writing this telephone note. Ms. Patel will know about the schedule change.
writing.hint: Join the clauses directly: '...note so that Ms. Patel will know...'
targetAnswers: I am writing this telephone note so that Ms. Patel will know about the schedule change.
I am writing this telephone note so that Ms. Patel knows about the schedule change.
writing.explanation: 'So that' expresses the purpose of the action and connects the two clauses.

writing.instruction: Rewrite the caller's statement as a reported phone message beginning with 'The caller stated that...':
writing.promptText: Direct words: 'I am calling about the invoice.'
writing.hint: Change 'I am calling' into reported speech using 'he was calling' or 'she was calling'.
targetAnswers: The caller stated that he was calling about the invoice.
The caller stated that she was calling about the invoice.
The caller stated that they were calling about the invoice.
writing.explanation: In reported speech, present continuous ('am calling') typically changes to past continuous ('was calling').

writing.instruction: Write a professional one-sentence response agreeing to take a message for your manager:
writing.promptText: Caller asks: 'Could I leave a message for Ms. Gomez?'
writing.hint: Start with 'Certainly' or 'Of course' and ask what the message is.
targetAnswers: Certainly, what would you like me to tell her?
Of course, what would you like me to tell her?
Certainly, please leave your message and I will pass it on.
Of course, I can take your message.
writing.explanation: A polite call recipient confirms willingness to help and prompts the caller for details.

writing.instruction: Rewrite this direct question as a very polite request using 'Would you mind':
writing.promptText: Can you send the contract again?
writing.hint: Remember to change 'send' to the gerund form 'sending'.
targetAnswers: Would you mind sending the contract again?
Would you mind sending me the contract again?
writing.explanation: 'Would you mind' requires an -ing verb form and ends with a question mark.

writing.instruction: Combine these two sentences into one using 'as soon as':
writing.promptText: Mr. Baker will return to the office. I will give him your message.
writing.hint: Place 'as soon as' before the present tense clause: '...as soon as he returns...'
targetAnswers: I will give him your message as soon as Mr. Baker returns to the office.
I will give Mr. Baker your message as soon as he returns to the office.
As soon as Mr. Baker returns to the office, I will give him your message.
writing.explanation: In time clauses referring to the future, use the present simple ('returns') after 'as soon as'.

writing.instruction: Correct the grammar and punctuation in this indirect question:
writing.promptText: could you tell me what time does the meeting start
writing.hint: Use statement word order ('the meeting starts') and capitalize the first word.
targetAnswers: Could you tell me what time the meeting starts?
Could you please tell me what time the meeting starts?
writing.explanation: Indirect questions do not invert the subject and auxiliary verb in the embedded clause.

writing.instruction: Transform this informal statement into a polite telephone opening using 'I am calling to':
writing.promptText: I want to confirm our appointment on Tuesday.
writing.hint: Replace 'I want to' with 'I am calling to'.
targetAnswers: I am calling to confirm our appointment on Tuesday.
I'm calling to confirm our appointment on Tuesday.
writing.explanation: 'I am calling to + base verb' is the standard professional formula for stating call purpose.

writing.instruction: Write a one-sentence reassurance telling the caller that Ms. Lee will receive the message today:
writing.promptText: Reassure the caller that Ms. Lee will get their message.
writing.hint: Use the formula: 'I will make sure Ms. Lee gets your message today.'
targetAnswers: I will make sure Ms. Lee gets your message today.
I'll make sure Ms. Lee gets your message today.
I will make sure that Ms. Lee gets your message today.
I will pass your message on to Ms. Lee today.
writing.explanation: 'I will make sure + person + gets the message' provides clear reassurance to callers.
